title: Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Review, Part 4 of 4 – Red, Green, & Scene Box Cards
content:
Space, the final frontier. These are the voyages of the starship Enterprise...as well as around 34 other new Spacecraft. Our continuing mission: To explore in detail the ramifications of newly-printed cardboard; to speculate upon their effects on formats such as Commander, Standard, & Modern; to boldly joke about the 43 new Creature types printed in this set unlikely ever to be seen again! Yes, Star Trek has arrived to Magic, and with it a host of new cards sure to shake things up. Most impactful is the full realization of Spacecraft as an Artifact subtype, more than doubling the number thusly printed. Today we're covering the set's red, green, and scene cards.

Star Trek officially releases to tabletop on November 13th, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on November 10th.

Red

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Brazen Bluff

Saffgor: This card is sweet, but it is also very likely...bad. Punisher effects like this always give you the worst possible option, and even in its best case scenario this is just a fancy ritual. Cast a bomb on the cheap, but spend a card to do so, or be a counterspell to a card your opponent doesn't care about. Really cool design, but this is part of a rather unfortunate lineage.

BPhillipYork: I love this card because it's fun, but the way actually playing it out will generally work isn't going to make it terribly strong.  Still, non-creature spells include enchantments and artifacts, so this could be a fun way to sneak out a conditional win enchantment during an opponent's turn.  The real problem is if your opponents think what you're doing are sufficiently threatening they'll just let you exile the spell, which means if you're trying to play it to free cast something you have to actually cast it on something you really want to counter.  Anyway, I think it'll lead to more fun games, and that makes a good card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain James T. Kirk

Saffgor: No Haste being granted makes me nervous about this, because being functionally a draw and a 1/1 for 3 mana, on the condition you're hellbent, doesn't inspire. Tersa Lightshatter compared to this guy just looks way better in essentially all formats.

BPhillipYork:  This seems fine, fun if you want to go balls out and have no cards in hand, still not that strong, generating officer tokens is useful for, well just tokens in general but also to enable things like Captain Benjamin Sisko to go nuts.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dominion Infiltration

Saffgor: I don't hate this card, but it feels like Devastating Onslaught tends to scale better. Cheaper for the first, the same for the second, and then it gets outpriced...but you get to plan around internal synergy, rather than relying on opposing options.

BPhillipYork:  This effects just don't ever really seem that worth it.  Only good if your opponents have really good creatures already or you have some wacky trick, and super expensive.

FromTheShire: 

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Encounter the Unknown

Saffgor: I mean this just seems unbelievable for 60-card, right? Instant-speed Pyroclasm that can be advantage if you're resource-light, that's just fantastic for midrange. It doesn't even hit Planeswalkers, so you can stick a Chandra and hold this up.

BPhillipYork:  Really solid utilitarian and value instant.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Erica Ortegas, Plucky Pilot

Saffgor: Fun Landfall enabler as a means to loop your triggers, especially with bouncelands. 4 mana is a bit dicey, but you could do worse if this ends up being a combo piece.

BPhillipYork:  This has potential for like, decks with lots of landfall triggers to just keep cycling lands back in and out, which is sometimes an issue for those decks, though graveyard play and fetchlands usually solves it.  Probably wouldn't recommend as a commander, because like, what you're going to ramp once you hit 4, sort of?  In mono-red?

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Exploratory Mission

Saffgor: The fact you're assured a nonland is great here, as it means Red isn't running out of gas. If this recoups mana, you're really happy with this effect. Look, I don't love this starting at 4 mana, but the actual effect is pretty stellar—if you're playing in Bracket 2, and have Landfall synergy, this goes in. It's going to effectively draw & pay for itself twiceover most games.

BPhillipYork:  This is nuts.  Like wtf.  Thankfully it's expensive enough to not be totally busted, but over any kind of long game, especially in stax type decks this is a crazy value engine.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Genesis Effect

Saffgor: This is mentioned as a sweet card for Pauper Wildfire, where you couple effects like this and Cleansing Wildfire with Indestructible Lands to ramp. Probably 2 copies make it in there, but I think this vastly improves that deck.

BPhillipYork:  I guess there's some neat things you can do with this, there's always the like, destroy indestructible land woohoo free land but for 5-mana, nah.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Infinite Diversity

Saffgor: I love what this card represents, but mechanically I am not its audience. This is a Timmy card, and that's okay.

BPhillipYork:  Infinity is like a lot bigger than what, 10?  12?  How many non-borg creatures are you likely to control at once?  Still, dangerous if you are able to cast some nasty instant a bunch of times, or just take like 7 extra turns.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Lwaxana Troi, Charming Guest

Saffgor: One-woman Roaming Throne, and I mean, I don't hate it! Lacking the Ward from the Throne is tough, and frankly I've found myself just...playing that card outside of typal, naming one of my Commander's types. This might be fine enough to sit in a similar role as far as that goes, but she's no Throne.

BPhillipYork:  Doubling triggers is nice, by default you're probably just targeting your commander, since your deck is built around them, and that can be fairly nasty.  Throwing this onto say Prosper, Tome-Bound is going to let you probably end the game that turn.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Naked Time

Saffgor: This might be the best card in the set for Standard from some early results, and while I don't love the art, at least it isn't Those Old Scientists. 2 mana ramp, into a pressure trigger, and then you shrug about that downside. The card's good, but it just does flat nothing once you've exited the early game, so I'm not sure about its merit. Jim Davis is on an Iroh, Tea Master donate deck with this, and that's...concerning.

BPhillipYork:  I don't uh.  I wouldn't probably play this card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Pah-Wraith

Saffgor: This not granting Haste keeps it from being a Land-based Craterhoof, but it remains a decent card to cheat out, I suppose.

BPhillipYork:  Well, that's basically a red sort of finisher creature, with the haste and buffing all your creatures for probably at least 4 or 5, which is pretty nice to have.  No trample and not handing out haste makes it a lot less equivalent to End-Raze Forerunners or other cards of that ilk.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Q, Stacking the Deck

Saffgor: Oh Q, what a shame it has been to brew you. Q was the very first card I covered in terms of Star Trek's new toys, and my final verdict—as it remains—is that he's more a fun puzzle to solve, than a deck to actually play. In any list that trims down to 1-5 nonlands, you just end up being a clock more than a person. Q basically can't be disrupted once he resolves, but because your gameplan from then on is so telegraphed, you tend to be focused down or otherwise played around like a force of nature, and not someone to politic with. Q robs you of options in play, even if he's a marvelous canvas in the deckbuilder.

BPhillipYork:  Yeah this is great.  Crazy.  Go hog wild.  Just like, see what happens, fun card.  Or do something boring and abusive and win the game but that's not very Q at all.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Quark, Humble Proprietor

Saffgor: What I love about Quark is that he quietly disincentivizes your opponents from attacking you on the ground in Commander, for fear of turning on your Treasures. Obviously they can be used for Improvise, Ghirapur Aether Grid, etc, but where Quark excels is in affording you time, and once you're unleashed after he dies, a truckload of mana. Great card.

BPhillipYork:  This is interesting, multiple ways now to just tap treasures for mana or other effects means this can be potentially pretty good, and you can always just sacrifice him or something.  Building up treasures that fast is pretty dangerous.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Tasha Yar, Out of Time

Saffgor: She doesn't belong in the Command Zone, but in the 99 of graveyard decks? Maybe, sure.

BPhillipYork:  You could definitely be looping this with things like Alesha, who smiles at death, or various other recursion schemes.  As a commander, like you could cast her, sacrifice somehow, then use the ability, but that's like 5 mana to net 2 exiled playable cards and then your commander tax is at 2, so is that good?  Final answer is no.  No it is not.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Will Riker, First in the Field

Saffgor: Now this is a Landfall Commander! Works like a charm with extra combats, forced end turn effects, and even stuff like Aggressive Mining. I am a huge fan of this design, and while Landfall isn't an especially exciting archetype, doing so in Monored breaks some fairly-new ground, especially at this power level.

BPhillipYork: So this is interesting, with all the lands from yard sources and landfall triggers this will generate a useful board state if you build around it, or enable landfall decks that include red.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Worf, Intelligence Contractor

Saffgor: Grab three things, chuck 'em at an opponent, then sacrifice them. Seems straightforward to me, and Worf seems great in any sacrifice deck that has Red.

BPhillipYork:  Where is Worf, beaten up by the adversary of the week to show how strong it is?  Crazy to imagine putting on that much makeup that many days of your life to most get used as a punching bag.  But, this is okay?  Steal and sacrifice or trade or something, flicker him I guess.

Green

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Jonathan Archer

Saffgor: Porthos lacking evasion is a shame, because otherwise this would have shades of Minsc & Boo. As it stands, I don't buy it.

BPhillipYork:  Making a legendary dog token is kind of old hat.  I guess some kind of reusable super giant growth is nice, nothing I'd really write home about but good if you have a particular creature you're going to be maybe double striking or something.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Kathryn Janeway

Saffgor: My goodness that's a lot of exploring. Twists and Turns, Topography Tracker, even Wildgrowth Walker just get an asinine amount of value from her, and all of those are now extremely findable given Enchantments can be tutored in Monogreen. I expect to see her at the LGS, and moreover, I expect to lose to her at least once in the first month following Star Trek's release. Bet on it.

BPhillipYork:  This is a very landfall focused commander that's like, all value no payoff, but in mono-green there's typically just more useful sorts of things.  But as an enabler in a landfall deck, it's pretty nuts, especially since with landfall triggers that generate token creatures this will trigger, letting you explore and potentially play another land, generating another trigger etc..

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

David and Carol Marcus, Creators

Saffgor: These get you a uniquely-named Land that can be duplicated with token doublers, and at worst are a source of 3-mana ramp. In the right deck, that's going to lead to a ton of Planet tokens.

BPhillipYork:  I guess you can like flicker them.  Token lands are a new thing, basically, and they do color fix which is kind of nice.  Almost no way I'd run this as a commander, I think my defacto would be more like in a reanimate deck where I wanted to sacrifice them for value.  For reasons .

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dr Joseph M'Benga

Saffgor: Just an uninspired design, but that doesn't make it a bad one. These are two strong effects stapled together on a Legendary Creature, so while the direction is clear and the nuance is absent, neither of those stop it from being a solid card at Bracket 2.

BPhillipYork:  Counter doublers are kind of boring but they do their thing, handing out hexproof also is pretty nice.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy

Saffgor: Holy shit is that a Green Undying Evil effect? That's new territory for the color as far as I'm concerned, and while the trigger being slow to return prevents a lot of combos, Flash does a lot of heavy lifting. Probably not a candidate for the Command Zone, but any deck with clones in Simic will have their eyes on McCoy.

BPhillipYork:  It's important that he can't return timelords.  But this is like, I dunno, sort of okay.  Maybe if I planning to beam him back up I guess it's useful holdable protection.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Final Frontier

Saffgor: This is the most disappointing card from the set, because they refused to print a single good, new Planet worth searching. The ones from Edge of Eternity remain your best options, and while Evendo is a fantastic piece it could have been so much better. 2 mana ramp from the yard is still probably good enough writ large, but I weep for what could have been (and might be, if they keep printing Planets).

BPhillipYork:  This is really below the curve of Kodama's Reach analogs, so mostly can be ignored.  Only real use is fetching Planets from the other space set.  The original space set if you will.  If you won't it's called Edge of Eternities and you'd probably be fetching Evendo, Waking Haven, or Uthros, Titanic Godcore.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Genesis Device

Saffgor: Scapeshift on a permanent that doesn't exile itself, my lord. See above for my woes on Planets, but this being a Scapeshift that grabs a Land to start with is pretty fantastic.

BPhillipYork:  Nice way to generate a huge amount of landfall triggers at once as a wincon.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Holo-Engineer

Saffgor: The 'instead' here is a concern, because it stops you from getting Treasures, Clues, etc. That, and being 4 mana, kills this guy for me.

BPhillipYork:  I mean, it's okay, I guess.  I feel like this card just exists for emergency hologram fanboys or something, like if you're generating a lot of tokens there are way better token replacers than getting 3/3 colorless illusions that are vanilla.  Only big upside is that they artifacts, and things could be done with that.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy

Saffgor:  Wears buffs well, is herself a buff as needed, and even adds the mana without need to tap. Seems great to me, especially in a post-Badgermole Cub ban world.

BPhillipYork:  This is going to give you parallel sort of ramp, basically another carpet of flowers, slower, but more impactful over time, though only green mana.  The backup ability to save something in a pinch, or get counters going, is super useful to have, especially if you draw into her late and don't really need the mana anymore.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

MACO Strike Team

Saffgor: I think this is better than Pawpatch Recruit? Not a 1:1 comparison, as it definitely has a worse ceiling without Offspring, but retaining a body on board if it's targeted seems like what decks playing this would want, more than just a counter.

BPhillipYork:  On paper it's like, oh wow.  But in practice getting 1/1s when your more valuable stuff gets blown up, isn't good.  Most targeted spells only target one thing, if you're routinely getting lots of your stuff targeted somehow, then it becomes okay.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Rok-Tahk, Budding Scientist

Saffgor: This adds 4 types for Federation you'd probably not have otherwise, and makes all your bodies into superdorks. Is that worth 6 mana? In the right deck, yeah, I could see it, but broadly speaking the Federation mechanic is on underwhelming enough cards as to reduce the allure of Rok-Tahk.

BPhillipYork:  If you have 6 mana, then you can be tapping your creatures for GG, reads like a win more card to me, mostly.  Maybe you generate a ton of tokens then use this to end the game, in which case, fine.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Saurian Explorer

Saffgor: {6}: Get a Landfall trigger. Horrifying with Agatha of the Vile Cauldron, obviously, but also quietly a mana outlet for any Landfall deck packing a combo. Scute Swarm and Ashnods also goes infinite readily with this, among other things. This card might be a common, but it's going to end games, mark my words.

BPhillipYork:  Well that's potentially a lot of planet tokens, for 6 mana, at some point you'll just have all the planets I guess.  But if you already have 6 mana, generally more mana isn't what you need, so much as something to do with 6 mana.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Stable Wormhole

Saffgor: This is a pretty absurd card to print at a glance, but I think it's weirdly pretty fair. Bit of extra ramp if you go to combat each turn, and while it does snowball a bit you do need to legitimately be aggressive if this is coming down turn 2/3, and you want to get max value.

BPhillipYork:  This seems like a potentially dangerous card in any game that goes long.  Just getting tons of value over time, it fits nicely into a stax strategy or anything that really slows the game down, since eventually people start missing land drops but you won't be missing planet drops.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Test of Courage

Saffgor: Amazing card for sideboards. About as flexible a card one can ask for at a single mana, at Instant-speed.

BPhillipYork:  Good instant speed green interaction is rare, this is more of it, and that is good.  Doesn't really do anything that new, but having both on one card is flexible.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Discovery, at Black Alert

Saffgor: I've had a Monogreen Spacraft-matter deck in paper since EOE, helmed by Maester Seymour, and this set was sure to bring some cool new toys for that. This is one of them, but in all honesty it may be such that this becomes the Commander of that strategy. This is a green Pantlaza if you squint, and while Monogreen has fewer mechanisms by which to repeat this effect, that's a lot of free value to contend with.

BPhillipYork:  Black alert?  That's dumb.  I'm so glad I didn't watch that dumb show.  So, discover 5 is really solid.  6 charges isn't that hard to attain, which makes this a strong value play over time, a 5/5 flyer is generally too big to be stopped easily and can, in a 4 player game probably generate it's discover triggers with pretty much impunity.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Voyager, Lone Wanderer

Saffgor: This is the most commonly-played version of Open the Way (a good card) that comes with an eventual body...oh, and you can flicker it. Obviously this is a great card, and any deck running 4 mana ramp will slot this in with gusto.

BPhillipYork:  It seems strange to me that this card doesn't really do a good job of encompassing what Voyager was about.  Like, if you fail to reveal any lands then you should get something (aka the Voyager got home).  But it's okay, grab 2 lands at 4 mana but you get 3/3 flyer is... fine.  You can flicker it so that's potentially a way to generate additional value.

Promos

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Borg Queen, Perfection Manifest

Saffgor: So they uh, hid one of the set's best Monoblack Commanders in the Welcome Decks. This is expensive but potent, and represents a pretty clear gameplan of running out small Artifact Creature hordes and a few massive stolen threats, all while reusing her via Undying Evil effects. No Finality counters either, meaning you can get back that same big threat over and over. I quite like this card, but why isn't it in the Borg Precon?

BPhillipYork:  This feels underwhelming for what the borg queen represented.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Badgey, Malicious Glitch

Saffgor: Fun card to twiddle, and can do some Pili-Pala loops well.

BPhillipYork:  Too expensive to be much other than a meme card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Divergent Timelines Scene Box

Saffgor: Bad news for the Abrams-verse fans: These cards are pretty bad, across the board. Chekhov and McCoy is likely the best among them, being a Terrasymbiosis in the Command Zone, but the rest just don't do enough. Uhura starts too expensive, Kirk is just an anthem, and Spock is probably outcompeted by the main set Uhura as a value engine for {2}{U}. Sulu has cute text which largely doesn't matter, and Scotty...I mean dude, if you want mass unblockable just give your board Horsemanship. I suppose he can give your opponents' Creatures unblockable? Is that the idea?

BPhillipYork:  Well Uhura is good, Sulu is good, Spock is potentially good, and Kirk, Man of Action goes well to support the real kirk, and I guess he buffs all of them, I dunno these don't really excite me that much.  Triptychs seem good enough, a six-tichs just seems overdone.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Enterprise-Q Scene Box

Saffgor: See this is how you do a Scene Box. Among these options, Troi, La Forge, & Q are standouts—Troi is an absolutely fantastic payoff for all of the White group hug draw, La Forge goes infinite in a number of ways, and Q obviously affords Faeries a genuine 5c option, on top of outrageous value. Even the worse of this set still have their uses, what with Picard making your Faeries enter as (at minimum) 3/3s, and Worf lets you swing out with a wide board. Data isn't great here, but he might just be reasonable enough in some of these other inexplicable Faerie typal Commanders. You could conceivably lead a powerful, interesting deck with 5/6 of these, and that's a pretty big win.

BPhillipYork:  This whole scene is much better thought out then the Kelvin timeline one.  And a lot more fun.  Q makes faeries and these guys benefit off of or make faeries and you use the faeries cast the cards in your decks, which is all fun and good and hangs togther.

Commander

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Beacon of Kahless

Saffgor: This is an okay 3 mana rock at worst, a pretty fantastic 3 mana rock if you swing out, and with extra combats this is making a wild amount of mana indeed. I'm quite bullish on the Beacon, but only for some very specific strategies. The one tragedy is this not working with Myriad, as is the case with all Battlefront cards.

BPhillipYork:  This is nice, solid, fitting the theme over the last few years of good 3 cost, colored, mana rocks.  Alongside things like Cursed Mirror, but stronger.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Grilka, Widowed Warrior

Saffgor: Go infinite with Aggravated Assault potentially using an opponent's Creature? That's pretty sweet, and Grilka does nasty things with cheap temporary clones on herself as well. 6 mana is a tough ask, but we got Queen's Diamond in the set, so...maybe?

BPhillipYork:  Too expensive unless you have some way to recur it endlessly.  Okay if you're going to cheat it out maybe and sacrifice what you borrowed.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Glory to the Empire!

Saffgor: 6 mana to always attack with 3 5/4s that turn, and likely afford your board +3/+3 on attack. This is a fun finisher for Bracket 2, and does its job well for that.

BPhillipYork:  Handing out melee is kind of dangerous giving how much the melee type triggers and myriad type triggers are starting to stack up.  6 is a lot of mana though, and there are typically stronger effects available, often on big fat creatures, for 6 mana.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Galvanizing Tenor

Saffgor: Seems like a decent piece for goad strategies, but the question there is 'how good is goad'. Really wish this also tapped its targets, or triggered when you attacked period, and not with it.

BPhillipYork:  This is fun, and annoying, but for 4 mana it's kind of low impact, but not big enough to be impossible to just block and kill.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Gagh Slinger

Saffgor: Warrior typal piece that will slowly rise in price due to its inability to be reasonably reprinted. Calling it now.

BPhillipYork:  Wow.  This is potentially really dangerous, what with cards like Najeela, the Blade Blossom existing.  Lots of ways to make warriors, and this will make each of them ping, and is also a cost reducer, which is pretty nice.  I think the whole klingon thing will be almost totally ignored.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Koloth, Tribble Hunter

Saffgor: This is analogous to Hansk, Slayer Zealot, but with none of the parts of that card which make it good. This card is bad outside of decks which care about goaded creatures, which Koloth does admittedly make a ton of.

BPhillipYork:  Okay, I kind of like this. Like hords of tribbles goaded and buffed is funny.  Not sure why these tribbles are bigger than the other tribbles, but who cares.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Own the Day

Saffgor: A 3-mana extra combat in the big '26. This card is just fantastic, and even gives you the extra Main phase too for all the shenanigans we'd hope. Outside of reprints this is likely going to be the best card from the Klingon precon.

BPhillipYork:  This is solid and well thought out, good in commander, rewards aggression and gives red a decent contingent type finisher.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Janice Rand, Essential Aide

Saffgor: If you have two Commaders via Partner/Backgrounds this is a truly absurd amount of ramp. It can't even fail, really, given it isn't nabbing basics like most ramp. It's a hard sell if you don't have 2 cards in the Command Zone, but among those lucky to be paired-up, Janice is your new best friend.

BPhillipYork:  This is really dangerous with partner, partner with, but also things like Derevi, Empyrial Tactician, or like Brago, King Eternal it's obviously out of color, but any kind of repeating flickering, or a commander that gets reanimated over and over will get kind of nuts.

That wraps up our look at the cards of Star Trek. We’ll be back next week with our regular content.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and more.

title: Autobattler RPG Next Fest: Five Games to Play
content:
The Steam Autobattler RPG Fest aka Games Designed in a Lab to Appeal to Jake Fest has begun! It is my solemn duty to play games that interest me and report to you fine folks if any of them are also worth your time. Here are five that stood out from the pack!

Guildrun

While this is still technically just a demo, I have been playing it consistently since it came out months ago. This game is one of the best autobattlers I’ve ever played. Straight up, it’s that good. The dev also does weekly updates to the demo while plugging along with the full game and there is absolutely enough here to satiate you. I have almost thirty hours of playtime in just the demo and still hop in every week to mess around.

If you have played Teamfight Tactics, then the game will be instantly familiar to you. Draft heroes, place them on the grid, equip them with items. Where it truly becomes special is in the heroes themselves. Each one has three different archetypes they can lean into, with even more room for creative teambuilding through various passives and items. Guildrun already has a space reserved in my games of the year for when it officially releases next year. Go play it.

Mechabellum

We’ve previously reviewed Mechabellum here, but I wanted to shout it out here as well since the trailer for this fest showcases it. It baffles me that this game hasn’t exploded everywhere yet because it has some of the deepest strategy of any game I’ve played. All of the strategic depth of an RTS like Starcraft 2 with none of the real time requirements.

The game plays in a very chess-like nature, with standard openings and build paths you’ll adopt as you play against other players or the recently added solo roguelike mode. You build a lot of swarming Crawlers, they adapt and bring swarm-killing Typhoons. You bring high single-target to kill the Typhoons, they build a swarm of light aircraft. On and on it goes until someone’s strategy is victorious. Play it as a fiercely competitive (and extremely challenging) solo mode, with a friend in 2v2, or as a roguelike. However you decide to play, you’ll love the strategy and the spectacle of big war machines exploding each other.

Slotbound

The wheel shall decide your fate. Create a group of heroes by spinning the slot machine and generating heroes based off the symbols you hit. Instead of the classic ‘combine three of the same hero into an upgraded version’, Slotbound lets any character freely absorb any other, inheriting passives that can shape their role on the automatic battlefield. Absorb the mace soldier to give another the chance to block. Absorb more maces to boost that ability, or absorb the duelist to get scaling attack speed as you attack. Absorb enough and you can change your class and start getting bonuses based on your factions like forest, tribal, and empire. The gameplay is simple, but a large meta-progression skill tree keeps you pulling that lever over and over.

Eslabong

Winner of the most fun name to say award, Eslabong is a fantasy gladiator sim. Purchase gladiators from dozens of classes, train them up, and have them compete in various modes for your glory. Standard mode is a 5v5, but in a season you can have the opportunities to enter solo tournaments, 8v8s, and wilder options like 2v2v2v2v2s and draft leagues.

You can either manually control the one gladiator you designate as captain of your squad, or let it be fully automated. There’s an extremely detailed tactics page you can change on the fly for each of your gladiators as well. Want to dive their healer and take them out early? Adjust your AI to focus on healer classes, never retreat, and never become distracted. Want your own healer to be in the thick of things for their AoE heals to be the most effective? Change to have their ai be close to teammates and prioritize hitting 2+ allies.

Off the battlefield, you can sell off your gladiators to other teams for big payouts and recruit prospects, analyzing them based on their stat growth potential and randomly generated abilities. You can get into the weeds of the management sim part of the game or just mash your gladiators into other teams and have a wonderful time either way.

Booster Pack Heroes

As a general rule, I tend to stay away from incremental games because I have a nasty habit of getting hyperfocused on them and having my entire day consumed. Booster Pack Heroes drew my attention because it appeared to have a bit more structure and goals than other incrementals I’ve played. The loop is simple: defend your tower from hordes of various enemies and unlock more and more different booster packs containing heroes. In between attempts, you can upgrade the rate you get boosters, the amount of damage your cursor does to enemies, and the heroes themselves in various ways.

Further into the game, you’ll unlock relics that boost certain types of heroes, as well as mechanical twists that alter your gameplay like the plane of death having no light save a small area around your cursor and your tower.

The full game took me about 6 hours to complete, which was a godsend for me because the loop was so compelling I physically could not put it down. If you have an evening to kill, I recommend you kill it with this.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Black Friday is back, and we've hunted down the best board game deals on Amazon
content:
Another year goes by, and Wargamer writes another article about Black Friday board games. It's tale as old as time, but we never get bored of seeing board games sold at a discount. However, we know how tiresome all that scroll-shopping can be. To save your poor thumbs the job, here's a curated list of the best deals - on Amazon US, at least.

If you're not fussed about price, our best board games guide is the ultimate list of titles worth your time. But, if you're on a tight budget, stick around:

Azul

44% off

Azul seems to go on sale every Black Friday, but we keep recommending it, because it's one of our favorite abstract strategy games. Ever. Period. This gorgeous tile drafting game about building eye-catching mosaics is easily learned, but mastery is a devious, delightful journey.

Check prices on Amazon

Everdell

26% off

Everdell is full of cutesy woodland creatures, but that doesn't mean it compromises on strategy. The iconic worker placement is an excellent brain-teaser, gorgeously presented on a multi-story board. It's a treat for any gaming veteran, but its high production quality means it might be the game that finally convinces your mom/dad/spouse/kids/little siblings to play a board game.

Check prices on Amazon

25% off

The Lord of the Rings: Fate of the Fellowship takes the classic c0-op game Pandemic and transforms it into an epic battle for Middle-earth. Both familiar and yet more formidable, this thematic game sends the Fellowship across the land, pushing back the forces of the Shadow wherever they meet. It's thrilling, stunning, and not to be missed at any price.

Check prices on Amazon

A Feast for Odin

25% off

A Feast for Odin is one of those titles every true board game fan should try once. It's a hefty game of resource management and grid placement. You'll recreate the classic life of a Viking, from daring sea expeditions to quiet agriculture. Throughout the year, you'll place your workers, gathering food and goods to stash in your longhouse. It's a gradual, satisfying engine builder with many paths to victory, and it's still one of the best examples of the genre, 10 years later.

Harmonies

41% off

Harmonies is our go-to comfort board game, a perfect light morsel for lunch breaks, quick gaming sessions, or evenings when you want to let your brain relax a little. The vibrant animal art, combined with a tactile, tactical drafting and tile placement session, is somehow both soothing and strategic. It's not to be skipped, especially with a steep discount.

Vantage

17% off

Vantage doesn't have a huge discount, but it's such a great time, it's worth picking up at any price. It's a co-op game where your only goal is to explore an unfamiliar planet. There's not even a true way to 'win' Vantage - the land is yours to potter around in as you see fit. With minimal yet extremely effective mechanics, Vantage is about the wonder of exploration, and no two games ever feel the same. There are few board games out there like it, and it's a must-play.

Cozy Stickerville

24% off

Cozy Stickerville is a recent title, and it's one of the top games we played in 2026. It's a charming legacy game, where you'll complete actions on cards at a leisurely pace. The decisions you make in response to the story decide what stickers you add to your lush green board - and these, in time, make up a town entirely unique to you. You can only ever play twice, but this fact stings less when you get your copy cheap.

Star Wars Villainous

50% off

Disney Villainous board games are a guaranteed crowd-pleaser for families and Disney-loving adults. Star Wars Villainous is a strong standalone in the series, giving you the chance to scheme as Star Wars' biggest villains. It's a light, compelling strategy game that's as easy to learn as it is to love.

Ra

30% off

Reiner Knizia has designed hundreds of board games, and many are considered all-time greats in the hobby. Ra is one of his most popular creations, an auction and set collection game where you bid on tiles to build monuments, advance technology or culture, and gain the favor of Egypt's Pharaoh. This game is almost 30 years old, but it still holds up today.

Cartographers

30% off

Cartographers is a stone-cold classic among board games. This roll-and-write tasks you with mapping a fantasy territory for your fickle queen. Over four seasons, you'll attempt to draw landmarks on the landscape that meet your queen's edicts, with the winner being whoever earns the highest reputation. It's snappy and strategic, and it's an excellent introduction to the roll-and-write genre.

Widely considered one of the best thematic games of all time, Spirit Island's current print run continues to dwindle, so the best time to try it is right now. Another recent gem, Star Wars: Battle of Hoth reimagines the classic Memoir 44, setting its immersive wargame gameplay on the snowiest planet in a galaxy far, far away. Approachable yet strategically rich, it doesn't innovate too much on the titles it grew from, but it's a fantastic addition to any war board game collection.

title: BattleTech IlClan List Overview: Federated Suns
content:
Greetings hereditary nobles and welcome back to List Overview! Last time we took a look at a strong Clan faction, the noble and bird-infested Clan Jade Falcon. This week we will swing to the other end of the cultural divide and look at an Inner Sphere power, the whipping boy of the IlClan period, the great, the mighty, the extremely delusional, Federated Suns!

When looking at a faction, it can be hard to figure out what sorts of things their availability wants you to do, and it can be harder still to make a force that really feels like it belongs to that faction. IlClan has made some significant strides compared to previous eras, with a good deal of faction specific mech variants and chassis that you can use as tentpoles to prop up a general conception of how a faction wants to fight, in ideal circumstances. While it can be fun to deviate from that here and there, this week we will take a look at what a bog standard stereotypical Fed Suns list would look like, and how you would go about playing it.

Lore Primer

Davion Heavy Guard force for an event. Credit: Jack Hunter

So, the Federated Suns. Once the most powerful state in the Inner Sphere, for a long time both in and out of universe it looked like the Federated Suns, led by the noble House Davion, were going to inevitably unite humanity under their "benevolent rule". However, compared to their height during the Clan Invasion, the Federated Suns are a shadow of their former selves come IlClan. The repeated hammer blows of the collapse of their personal union with the Lyran Commonwealth, the resulting civil war, the Word of Blake Jihad, and the HPG blackout badly weakened their state. This left them in a fragile position when their system of absolute rule by a single family (nigh universal in BattleTech's setting, to be fair) produced an insane lunatic who very nearly led the realm into ruin, culminating in the capture of their capital planet by their historical rivals, the Draconis Combine.

While the Federated Suns have recaptured New Avalon and are finally under semi-competent rule again, they are still in a battered state and desperate situation, with enemies on all sides sharpening knives to finally finish off the Davion devils. This is a large reversal from the historical trend for the Federated Suns to be the hegemonic heroes of BattleTech, knights in shining BattleMechs come to liberate the Inner Sphere to a slightly less repressive autocratic system. That shining armor is dented and battered, but you do have to admire the spirit to keep kicking, screaming, and biting the whole way down no matter how awful things have gotten for them.

In terms of how their military is said to fight, there is a heavy focus on Autocannons, with nearly all Fed Suns specific mechs mounting at least one of them on their primary configuration. In addition, they are rich, well equipped, and for the longest time they were at the bleeding edge of Inner Sphere technology. While that technical lead has all but disappeared by IlClan, their love of autocannons refuses to be extinguished and they still have a large amount of former testbeds in their inventory deployed as line units.

You might want to play the Federated Suns in IlClan if you love autocannons, special munitions, and the fantasy of bitter resistance while surrounded by enemies looking to get even with you.

Availability

The Federated Suns availability is quite fun come IlClan. They have a large amount of faction specific units that are extremely strong under Core Rules. As the inventor of Precision and Armor-Piercing Autocannon ammunition, they maintain a large amount of basic and light autocannons in their mech inventory and can make fantastic use of those special ammo types. Their faction specific mechs, in particular the Templar, Templar III, Argus, and Inferno, are all priced to move and extremely mean for the cost. Faction specific variants are also strong with many of them originating as Civil War/Jihad era experiements that have reached mainline production, such as the Longbow 13NAIS, Thunderbolt 9Nr and 9NAIS, the Enforcer III NAIS, honestly anything with NAIS in the name.

There is a through-line with most of these mechs, which is BV efficiency. Davion mechs tend to come cheap. Autocannons are dirt cheap in BV and their faction specifics tend to be slow and extremely durable, which BV is kind to. In addition, they get access to the Blood Asp and Regent, two of the game's better Clan assault mechs for a given amount of BV. While you can go fast and light, the Davion Availability tends to push you towards their BV efficient 4/6 and 5/8 heavies and assaults. These mechs are extremely reliable and rugged, and this makes the faction fairly merciful to players of moderate experience. You have to make some positioning calls and deploy smartly due to that low speed, but you get enough armor per BV that it is unlikely you can make a minor mistake bad enough to be game ending.

Anyways, enough about the broad strokes, lets get specific and go over the list I built to bring as much Davion character and charm as possible while still putting your opponents in the ground.

The List

This Scale 4 list consists of the following mechs, all at 4/5 skills

  • Nightstar NSR-9FC, 1929 BV
  • JagerMech JM7-DD, 1690 BV
  • Axman AXM-4D, 1222 BV
  • Argus AGS-6F, 1524 BV
  • Thunderbolt TDR-9Nr, 1635 BV

This comes in at exactly 8000 BV on the dot, which pleases me. In addition, every mech here save the Thunderbolt is primarily armed with autocannons. They also all are faction specific to the Federated Suns in IlClan and aren't on any other major power's availability. The Nightstar and Thunderbolt do show up on Mercenary, but that is it. This is as Davion of a list as it is possible to build, and a list you genuinely can't build anywhere else.

Nightstar NSR-9FC

Nightstar. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Nightstar is, as you might know, one of Liberty's favorite mechs. While this is not the Nightstar he prefers, it is still an exceptionally strong assault mech. Moving 4/6, it carries an effective weapon load with 2 LB 10X autocannons, an ER PPC, and 3 medium lasers. With a solid firing pattern of "Everything but one laser", the 9FC is your centerpiece in this list, able to lean on its thick armor and sheer mass to bully smaller mechs to death while still coming in at less than 2000 BV. For deployment and use, identify the central objective and run towards it, drawing fire away from the rest of your list and outputting the same damage as an Awesome 9Q on a much faster, meaner frame.

For the LBs, you have way more than enough ammo for a normal game. Fire solid shot until their are open locations on your target, then swap to cluster to exploit the great big holes the rest of your list is opening up for you. This is your main crit-seeker and source of cluster hits, so make sure you are keeping that in mind and taking advantage of that flexibility.

JagerMech JM7-DD

JagerMech. Credit: Rockfish

Delta Delta here is a mech I have been absolutely in love with lately. Turning the usual JagerMech/Rifleman script on its head, the JagerMech is a tough, mean motherfucker of an all rounder. Mounting a pair of Clan UAC/10s as its primary weapons alongside a pair of LAC/5s and ER medium lasers, it outputs a genuinely fantastic amount of damage for the BV. While Ultra Autocannons are not terribly reliable, when they work they really work.

In addition, while the DD is full of ammo, CASE II goes a long way towards making that almost a non-issue. You also have enough ammo to carry both precision and AP in the LAC/5s, and you should. Having access to both ammo types is strong, and AP can absolutely save your ass if you come up against Hardened or Ballistic Reinforced armor.

For use, the DD wants to move up alongside the Nightstar and Axman, focusing its fire with them and generally being a max armor 70 tonner at your enemy. Normally a JagerMech would want to hang back and plink, but Delta Delta is a strong and independent fire support mech that doesn't need a frontline, it is the fucking frontline. The JagerMech as a chassis has a reputation as a poorly armored shitbot, and you can use that reputation to keep fire off of it as it pummels the enemy's frontline the fuck to death. It can also flip its arms and put UACs and Precision LACs behind it, which will make any enemy Fire Moths very, very sad.

Axman AXM-4D

Axman. Credit: Rockfish

The 4D is one of my two favorite Axmans, and I am a connoisseur of Axmans. Costing basically nothing and carrying quad LAC/5s, a pair of medium lasers, just enough ammo, and a targeting computer, the 4D is here to dispense 5 pointers and axe murder its way through the enemy's list. With a reasonable heat build of movement heat on an alpha, you do need to be careful around Infernos due to the single heat sinks that this mech carries. For 1222 BV it is almost impossible to get more mech though, and if you can bait correctly you can spread damage out between this, the JagerMech, and the Nightstar, keeping all 3 of them alive for much longer than their XL engines would otherwise imply.

In addition, if a mech has to stand on an objective or draw fire, the Axman is your main guy for that. It is tough enough to stand up to a Kodiak or other nightmare DPS machine for a couple turns and buy time for the rest of your list to hopefully pummel said nightmare mech the fuck to death. It is hard to trade down with a 4D, any heavy or assault mech you can trade its life for is going to be a positive value trade for you. You should be looking to trade it aggressively, and in all honesty AP ammo is great for this. Most opponents will get extremely scared when they start taking 4 TAC attempts a turn all at a -1 to hit bonus, so you should almost always be able to draw fire onto the 4D. Overall a solid piece of your frontline and one of the game's absolute best heavy mechs for the BV spent.

Argus AGS-6F

Argus. Credit: Rockfish

Another absolute all-star, the Argus 6F is part of an extremely elite club. It is one of the only 3 basic AC/20 mechs in the game that goes faster than 4/6, and a 5/8 AC/20 is a scary goddamn thing. It only competes with the Thunder 1L and a random Dragoon variant that only exists during the Star League Civil War era. Use case for the 6F is extremely simply. Load half the bins with Precision, the other half with AP, and run next to people and murder them. While your 3 4/6 mechs are pushing up the mid field to secure an objective, the Argus and Thunderbolt should be looking to do one of two things.

If there is a second objective you need to seize, the two of them should try to take it. If they run into trouble at that second objective, you have the mobility to flee back towards the main body of your force. Compared to many other list's flanking/second objective forces you will usually have a hell of a lot more mass than them to bully them off of an objective, and a Precision AC/20 acts as a phenomenal flyswatter for any Locust IICs, Fire Moths, or Phantoms that decide to come fuck with you.

If there isn't a viable second objective to fight over, the Argus and Thunderbolt just need to hang back a bit until the frontline engages and then run in to pull aggro and pull some nasty flanks, piling damage onto damaged targets and exploiting any back arcs they can find.

Thunderbolt TDR-9Nr

Thunderbolt. Credit: Rockfish

The perfect companion to the Argus, the 9Nr is another fantastic 5/8 Davion cavalry heavy. Mounting a large VSP laser as its main weapon, it backs that up with a trio of ER medium lasers, a Light PPC, and a Streak 6. It also carries a full EWAR suite with a Bloodhound probe and an ECM. There are also B-Pods in it so that you can clown on Battle Armor, which is a lot of fun.

The VSP and ER lasers are your main firing pattern, and it is safe to chuck the Streak on every once in a while if you are willing to go to 4/6 for a turn. You just want to follow along with the Argus and do all the same flanky things, but there is a slight difference with the Thunderbolt. If the enemy has ATMs or a large amount of Artemis missiles, you should make absolutely sure that you keep your entire list within 6 hexes of the Thunderbolt. That ECM can shave huge amounts of damage off of an ATM or Art Missile volley, and it will pay for itself rapidly if you can make use of it.

Gameplan

Bits and pieces of this have been scattered throughout the mech sections, but as a whole this list wants to use its mass and armor to bully your opponent. You will almost always be heavier, nastier, meaner, and more heavily armored than any given opposing force. Your damage up close is strong, but this list still has some substantial teeth at medium ranges and falls off gracefully. In general you would love to be able to make a big old ball of mech in the middle of the board and slam forwards, making tons of physical attacks and drowning them in nasty autocannon hits. Many missions though are going to have objectives spread across a map, and those can be a bit of a struggle. My advice for missions like that is that you can only really fight to contest two objectives, one with the 4/6s and one with the 5/8s.

If your opponent goes wide to every objective, you should have local superiority of firepower and mass on both of the objectives you are fighting over, letting you secure the points from both of those and try to make up the difference on the objectives you can't contest by murdering anything that comes close to you. You will frequently be outmanuevered but rarely outgunned, outnumbered, or outmassed. Do not be tempted to peel individual mechs off to do side objectives or anything, you need to stay together.

For Core Missions, you want to play the various Deathmatch missions (Ambush, Annihilation, Dominate, Extraction, Focal Point, and General Melee) by just making a big ball and running forwards into your enemy. The other missions are a little rougher for this list than one that has a heavier light mech presence, but the Thunderbolt's electronics and the fact that 3 out of your 5 mechs have hands should give you sufficient tools to play with. You want to, as mentioned, try to split into two groups to hold 2 objectives. You really can't afford to go wider than that. If you need to have a mech hang back on an objective away from the fight, the Axman is probably your best choice for that. It has decent enough range on its LACs and it is your cheapest unit. If there are objectives you can pick up and move, use the Thunderbolt to pull them over to the rest of your list..

Final Thoughts

The idea of this list was to use the unique, strong Davion exclusive mechs to go wide with heavy mechs and bully people. You can easily survive the death of any single one of your mechs and keep going, and nothing is an irreplaceable lynchpin. While you won't win a 1v1 with a Kodiak with anything in your list, you should never, ever be fighting a 1v1 if you can help it.

At Scale 4 the Fed Suns are a very strong faction in general, they have a huge amount of very good 1000-2000 BV mechs that do a whole hell of a lot for the price. Most factions need to concentrate BV in some more expensive units at Scale 4, and end up with some medium and light mechs to make up the difference. The Fed Suns have a very strong heavy mech spam archetype, and this is only one example. Building around the Templar III and Inferno is a very valid alternative, and you can get up to some really goofy shenanigans with an AC/10 maxxing strategy.

This list is fairly beginner friendly and simple to pilot, the main thing to keep in mind is that you absolutely need to keep your mechs together in at most 2 groups. Individually you are mediocre, but through the power of teamwork you can equal or surpass any opponent.

Also I just love autocannons so much. Shoot people with autocannons. It will do you a lot of good. Its therapeutic and good for the soul.

And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Is a D&D Owlbear biologically possible, or is the famous monster just fantasy?
content:
Of all the monsters available in Dungeons and Dragons' big bestiary, one has always fascinated me for how simple yet ludicrous it is: the owlbear. It's a classic and imposing chimera of a design, but so funny if you think about it for even a moment. What advantage could an owl's head possibly provide on a bear's body? Wouldn't you be better off, in pretty much every way, with just a standard bear?

Obviously everything in D&D can be handwaved away with 'a Wizard did it', but it's much more fun to think how something like this could have arisen naturally. And I don't think the answer is an amorous encounter between an adventurous bear and a very brave owl. Could an owlbear, a strange amalgamation of bird and beast, realistically evolve through the forces of natural selection?

Maybe! Right away, I think I have a plausible animal group narrowed down for this experiment. One which had a beak, and which scientists initially thought had to be a hoax thanks to its combination of mammal and bird-like features. Owlbears are quite clearly monotremes!

Beaks are common, useful structures found across multiple disparate groups, from squid, to birds, to fish. And often, as happened in birds and beaked reptiles like turtles, an animal goes from toothed to beaked, gradually losing its gnashers until it's doing all its cutting and crunching with a hard beak instead. But because mammals have developed much more specialized teeth than other vertebrates, with different shapes and sizes adapted for different roles, they very rarely give them up.

But monotremes (represented today by the platypus and the echidna) are one of the rare exceptions. They lost their teeth and - rather than the keratinized structures of other beak-bearers - developed a rubbery beak-like snout, which is not only used for feeding, but also gives them superpowers. They have special sensors within, designed to detect the electrical signals of their prey, just like sharks can.

While most useful underwater, perhaps an owlbear could use this to hunt down rabbits or adventuring parties too. Even at peak diversity, none have ever become large apex predators, but all monotremes are carnivores.

It seems plausible to me that an owlbear could be some distant relative of the echidna, an animal which already has the rough body shape of a bear - check out the Murrayglossus, an echidna from the Pleistocene that was over three foot long - if you don't believe me. This would explain the sharp claws, the beak, and the feathers. Okay, that last one might need more unpacking.

I think an owlbear's feathers could be derived from the hardened spines of an echidna-esque ancestor. Actually, this is one of its few owl traits that could be eminently useful. Owls are some of the most-feathered birds in the world, and this major fluffiness, as well as a serrated edge on the feathers which breaks up airflow, is what enables their super silent flight. Bears are already surprisingly stealthy considering their massive bulk, with soft foot pads and a flat-footed gait. So my hypothesis is that, while initially serving as spines for defence, the owlbear's hairs may have gradually changed to their current feather-like appearance to help it sneak up on prey: a classic case of convergent evolution.

Obviously, we can assume its ancestors gradually started going after larger prey, and this allowed its body size to scale up in turn. But we have to take a bit more of a logical leap to explain how the tube-like snout of an echidna might become the sharpened beak of an owl(bear).

Monotremes have soft, rubbery beaks, not at all suitable for tearing flesh, and in fact they rely on keratinous pads on their tongues and inside their mouths to 'chew' their invertebrate food. You can forget about shearing through bone. But my guess is that it's this keratinous pad, not the fleshy 'bill' at all, that forms the owlbear beak.

In the transition from a semi-aquatic lifestyle to a terrestrial, burrowing one, echidnas lost many of the electroreceptors in their beak, which may make it easier for it to be lost altogether. Perhaps, as owlbear ancestors started to eat larger animals like lizards or stirges, the spiked pad grew larger, and became more prominent, until it actually extended from the bill and ultimately replaced it entirely. Essentially, the owlbear rebuilt the beak from scratch. Obviously, it would have to lose electroreception for this to work, but that ability functions far better in the water anyhow, since air is less conductive.

So there we have it! A logical owlbear, forged through the powers of speculative evolution. Their beaks, feathers, body-structure, and egg-laying, can all be explained by their close relationship with the echidna.

I wonder if they also have four-headed penises? I'll let you do the Googling on that one.

title: Big game hunting in Warhammer 40k - Kastelan Robots are cheap and lethal
content:
Earlier this week, players in the r/WarhammerCompetitive subreddit asked the question, "how do you one-shot a Telemon Dreadnought?" This walker has a strong claim to be the hardest unit in Warhammer 40,000 for its points cost, and the results of their brainstorming session made for an interesting who's who of the most dangerous units and combos in the game. Since then I've found more great suggestions on how to bring down the beast, particularly from Custodes players who have been on the receiving end of a beating. The most interesting candidate so far? The Adeptus Mechanicus' Kastelan Robots.

The Telemon is such a difficult target to kill because it stacks so many overlapping defenses: 2+ armor and a 4++ invulnerable save, a penalty of -1D against enemy ranged attacks, a Martial Ka'tah ability that inflicts -1 to hit it in melee, an enhancement that gives it Feel No Pain 5+ against all damage, T11, and 14 wounds. Including the enhancement, that comes out to 310 points. There may be tougher bricks in other Warhammer 40k factions, but for the price, the Telemon is unparalleled.

Alone, a unit of four Kastelan Robots with an attached Cybernetica Datasmith will kill a Telemon in one round of combat more often than it doesn't. We're not talking about a guaranteed kill here, but that package comes in at the low, low price of 320 points - and there are ways to buff it further.

Equipped with paired Kastelan Fists, the robots start out with four twin-linked WS 4+, S12, AP-2, D3 melee attacks each. But this is the Ad Mech: we're going to stack some buffs.

The Datasmith can activate Conqueror Protocols to grant the Kastelans +2 Attacks each, and the armywide Conqueror Imperative can grant them +1WS. The Cohort Cybernetica detachment gives access to the Machine Superiority stratagem, which lets you ignore all stat penalties, and now the Telemon's Martial Ka'tah penalty to hit isn't in effect.

From 24 attacks the Kastelans should land 16 hits, a meaty 14.22 wounds, 7.11 of which will go through the invulnerable save; then after Feel No Pains, we land an average of 14.22 damage overall - closer to 14.5 if we add in the Datasmith's puny punches. So on average dice, Kastelans wipe the Telemon.

To guarantee the kill, Belisarius Cawl has to help out. This is a 220 point model who every competitive Ad Mech player fields, as the Invocation of Machine Vengeance grants re-rolls to hit against a designated target each turn. That puts the Kastelans' average result up to 21.33 hits and a much more comfortable 18.96 damage.

Compared to the original list of Telemon hunters, I rank the Kastelans alongside the Knight Lancer. The Lancer has a better chance to kill the Telemon unaided more than the Kastelans, but they can pull it off more often than not, and they're 125 points cheaper. And how many points is one turn of Belisarius Cawl's attention really worth…?

Part of what makes the Kastelans such incredible value in this match up is that they don't pay for anything they don't need. Their fists have AP-2, exactly enough to push the Telemon back on its invulnerable save; they've got S12 attacks, just enough to wound the Telemon on 3+.

Another useful factor is the variety of buffs the Kastelans have access to. They can easily gain an extra -1 AP from the Conqueror Imperative by standing close to a Battleline unit, which they don't need into the Telemon but can make use of against targets without invulnerable saves. And Machine Superiority is actually even more useful against another dreaded brick of a unit, 10 Terminators led by Darnath Lysander.

Lysander's Icon of Obstinacy inflicts -1 to hit his unit; in the Terminator Storm Force detachment the 2CP Stratagem Tactical Dreadnought Fortitude reduces incoming damage from attacks in any phase by 1; and if the Marine player doesn't have two command points, they'll likely have access to Armour of Contempt for one. Machine Superiority ignores all these debuff-based defenses.

The Kastelans still won't wipe the unit - with Cawl's help they might clear all ten terminators, but Lysander will be standing, especially if he's used his once per game 2++ invulnerable save. And if he's brought Assault Terminators carrying +1 Wound storm shields, forget about it…

The Kastelans don't have the scariest damage output of all units we've considered so far, but they are the cheapest yet, and they can do the most with the least support. If you haven't faced the Martian rock'em sock'em robots, beware!

Got a suggestion for an unkillable defender or an irresistible attacker? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Whale card on MTG's Reserved List sees 290% price spike, hitting $90
content:
An ancient MTG card and rare on the Reserved List has spiked in price. Great Whale is a blue creature from the 1998 set Urza's Saga which cost around $23 for a near mint card in July of this year. Now, the best condition copies have spiked 290%, with many selling for $90.

A seven mana card that untaps seven lands, Great Whale is one of many blue 'free' spells that pay for themself by granting you mana back. It's a powerful ability, but unlike other, similar Urza's block cards like Frantic Search, this one has been largely forgotten.

Partly that's because its place on the Reserved List means it can't be reprinted and is much more expensive than its effect is worth, and partly that's because its seven mana cost makes it a hard-to-reach way to gain this effect. Peregrine Drake from the same MTG set does the same thing, but only costs five mana (to untap five lands) so all the combo Commander decks that make infinite mana by flickering an untapping creature, use the far cheaper and less mana intensive drake instead.

However, there's an underwater set on the horizon, the first stop on the 2027 MTG release schedule, and this is why Great Whale is spiking. The set's First Look on November 13 revealed there'd be a cycle of whale gods, one for each color, but if you look at TCGPlayer, you'll see this isn't when sales started flying and the price skyrocketed. Instead, that happened on November 16, and it was due to a leak. If you want to remain unspoiled, stick your fingers in your ears now (actually, that won't help).

The two face commanders for the Sultai deck Terrors of the Abyss were leaked on the 16th, revealing two legendary creatures that work with 'Sea Monsters'. What's a sea monster? Well, it's a new batching term like outlaws or party, which refers to krakens, leviathans, octopuses, serpents… and whales. A shorthand way of grouping these creature types together, and a sign that Wizards plans to make a bunch of synergies for them.

There are actually already several cards in Magic that specifically refer to krakens, leviathans, octopuses, and serpents, but the leak revealed that whales are now going to be lumped in with them too, making a card like Great Whale much more interesting. In fact, both Terrors of the Abyss leaders offer easy ways to cheat the card into play.

What are you most excited for about Nauctis - the cute animal people, the merfolk, or the big monsters? Let us know on the Wargamer Discord.
