title: All official DnD races and species explained
content:
DnD races represent the different species found in the world's oldest tabletop RPG. Your DnD species (as they've been recently re-named) decides your appearance and culture, but it also determines rules-relevant facts about your size, speed, and abilities.

There are dozens upon dozens of official Dungeons and Dragons races, though the current Player's Handbook features just 10. Whether you want to play a standard species or something rarer, your choice has a big impact on your character. I've painstakingly researched each possible option and explained how they work in this guide.

Before you start shopping for a new species, a few housekeeping rules. D&D 5e now has its own refreshed sub-edition, 5.5e. Some species appear in both, but others don't. I've made it clear where you can find the most up-to-date version of each option. For brevity's sake, I've also only presented the most recent rules - though I've listed other, older sourcebooks you can investigate yourself if you prefer 2014 to 2024.

Also, this isn't my only guide to character creation. I recommend checking out Wargamer's guides to DnD classes and DnD backgrounds, as they complement the character options here pretty well! Okay, now we're ready to begin:

The core DnD races are:

  • Aasimar
  • Dragonborn
  • Dwarf
  • Elf
  • Gnome
  • Goliath
  • Halfling
  • Half-Elf
  • Half-Orc
  • Human
  • Orc
  • Tiefling

All DnD races include:

  • Aasimar
  • Dragonborn
  • Dwarf
  • Elf
  • Gnome
  • Goliath
  • Halfling
  • Half elf
  • Half orc
  • Human
  • Orc
  • Tiefling
  • Aarakocra
  • Astral Elf
  • Autognome
  • Bugbear
  • Centaur
  • Changeling
  • Deep Gnome
  • Dhampir
  • Dracthyr
  • Draenei
  • Duergar
  • Duskling
  • Earthen
  • Eladrin
  • Fairy
  • Firbolg
  • Genasi
  • Giff
  • Githyanki
  • Githzerai
  • Goblin
  • Hadozee
  • Harengon
  • Hexblood
  • Hobgoblin
  • Kalashtar
  • Kender
  • Kenku
  • Kobold
  • Leonin
  • Lizardfolk
  • Lorwyn Changeling
  • Loxodon
  • Lupin
  • Minotaur
  • Owlin
  • Plasmoid
  • Reborn
  • Rimekin
  • Satyr
  • Sea Elf
  • Shadar kai
  • Shifter
  • Simic Hybrid
  • Tabaxi
  • Thri kreen
  • Tortle
  • Triton
  • Vedalken
  • Verdan
  • Warforged
  • Yuan ti

Aasimar

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Warlock, Paladin
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Thanks to a shared ancestry with celestials, each Aasimar is blessed with divine looks and abilities. They're naturally resistant to necrotic and radiant damage, plus they're gifted healers who can roll d4s equal to their proficiency bonus to restore a creature's HP.

All Aasimar can cast the Light cantrip using Charisma as their spellcasting modifier, which implies the optimal builds for this species rely on that stat. However, if you're happy to sacrifice this (very situational) cantrip, an Aasimar can excel in any D&D class.

The Aasimar's most explosive feature is Celestial Revelation. When activated, this can give your Aasimar a fly speed, create a ten-foot emanation of light that deals radiant damage, or force enemies to make a Charisma save or become frightened. Whichever form they take, it lets the Aasimar deal additional radiant or necrotic damage when they attack.

Learn more in our full Aasimar species guide.

Dragonborn

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Charisma (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Barbarian, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Dragonborn resemble humanoid dragons, though D&D lore flip-flops on exactly how this species got its draconic features. However it happened, the Dragonborn's scaly, wingless appearance makes them one of the most recognizable species.

Their signature Breath Weapon helps in that department, too. Able to exhale a force of destructive energy that deals 1d10 damage on a failed Constitution saving throw, they've got an ace in the hole straight out of the gate. Its damage and difficulty class will increase as they level up, and your choice of Draconic Ancestry will determine its damage type, as well as your character's damage resistances.

The Dragonborn also benefits from 60 feet of Darkvision. More excitingly, once they reach level five, they can grow wings as a bonus action to gain a fly speed. We'd recommend this species for martials that usually lack ranged options and mobility.

Learn more in our DnD Dragonborn species guide.

Dwarf

SizeMedium
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Fighter, Barbarian, Druid
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Originally members of cave-dwelling clans, the DnD Dwarf species has a reputation for durability and a handy way with stone. Mechanically, this manifests as a resistance to poison damage and advantage on saving throws against being poisoned.

Dwarfs also have the Dwarven Toughness feature, which automatically increases their maximum hit points by one, and it does so again with every DnD level up. It doesn't get much more durable than that. Unsurprisingly, the classes that tend to suit a Dwarf are those looking to keep themselves standing on the front lines of battle.

Beyond this, a Dwarf's skills are defined by their ancient tendency to yearn for the mines. They have extended Darkvision (120ft rather than the standard 60ft) and tremorsense for 60 feet instead of enhanced History rolls when checking out pieces of rock - far more useful, if you ask us.

Learn more in our complete DnD Dwarf guide.

Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Wizard, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tall, sleek, and pointy-eared, The DnD Elf is a graceful being, most at home in ethereal forests. Their Darkvision and proficiency in either Insight, Perception, or Survival make them excellent stealthy scouts. Elves also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and they enter trances instead of going to sleep at night.

Each Elf has an Elven Lineage that decides some of their natural abilities. This makes the Elf an immensely flexible species, perfect for many kinds of characters (though, most of the time, we tend to recommend it for spellcasters).

Drow have enhanced Darkvision, and they can cast Dancing Lights, Faerie Fire, and Darkness. High Elves know Prestidigitation, Detect Magic, and Misty Step - though they can swap the cantrip with another from the Wizard spell list each day. Wood Elves have a base speed of 35 feet, as well as the ability to cast Druidcraft, Longstrider, and Pass Without Trace.

Learn more in our DnD Elf species guide.

Gnome

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWizard, Rogue, Artificer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Vibrant and expressive, DnD Gnomes are often styled as a curious and cunning race that enjoys the thrill of adventure. However you choose to roleplay them, all Gnomes gain the same basic benefits - Darkvision, plus advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws.

When you decide to play a Gnome, you'll choose a specific Gnomish Lineage. Forest Gnomes are illusionists who can speak to small beasts (often without wasting a spell slot). Meanwhile, Rock Gnomes can cast Mending and Prestidigitation, and they can still tinker with tools to create a small mechanical device.

A species that gains extra spells is usually a surefire pick for a spellcasting class, as it beefs up their existing repertoire. The Rogue is our wildcard suggestion, though. Gnomes are great at finding non-violent solutions to problems, which pairs well with the Rogue's utility-focused approach.

Learn more about this species in our DnD Gnome guide.

Goliath

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet (2014) or 35 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

A DnD Goliath may only be slightly bigger than your average human, but they have strength that rivals their Giant ancestors. They're as durable as granite, and they make for great martial characters.

The Goliath has advantage on checks against the grappled condition, and from level five onwards, they can become Large for 10 minutes, which gives them advantage on Strength checks and increases their speed by 10 feet, as well as greatly enlarging the area they affect in combat. Hulk, smash!

Additionally, the Goliath chooses one ability that's unique to their Giant Ancestry. This might allow them to teleport as a bonus action, deal extra damage, slow or knock enemies prone, or even reduce the damage the Goliath takes. Giant Ancestry is so versatile that you could play six or seven Goliaths and not have one feel same-y.

Learn more in our DnD Goliath guide.

Halfling

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Bard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Halflings are almost identical to the Hobbits of Tolkien's Middle-earth, though without the thick foot hair and round front doors. Living in peaceful, bucolic communities usually hidden from the conflicts of the world, they're cheerful and curious.

Halflings are extra nimble, able to move through the space of any creature that's at least one DnD size larger than them. They're also brave, with advantage on saves against the frightened condition, and lucky, meaning they're able to reroll any 1 on a d20. As well as luck and courage, Halflings have stealth to fall back on, as they can Hide as long as they're obscured by a creature at least one size larger than them.

All kinds of characters benefit from extra luck, but we tend to build Halfling characters that get maximum value from their stealth and mobility. That means Scout characters and anyone who needs an easy way to escape mid-fight.

For a full description, check out our DnD Halfling guide.

Half-Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 any other stat (2014 rules only)
Best forBard, Sorcerer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

Born of Human and Elf parents, DnDHalf-Elf characters take bits from both of their ancestral lines. Thanks to their Elf lineage, they have Darkvision and are immune to being put to sleep. They also have the versatility of Humans, which gives them proficiency in two extra DnD skills.

Like Elves, Half-Elves have a subrace that can give them further powers. However, if you want to take the optional features of a Drow, High, or Wood Half-Elf, you must sacrifice the extra skill proficiencies granted by your Human ancestry. In their place, you can learn additional spells, become trained in additional weapons, or gain a swimming speed.

Species of dual parentage like the Half-Elf and the Half-Orc (who we'll discuss in a moment) weren't included in the 2024 Player's Handbook, so you'll only have the 2014 version to work with. Still, their flexible DnD stats and skills make them strong Charisma casters. The Bard is our top choice of class for the species overall.

Want to learn more? Here's our full DnD Half-Elf species guide.

Half-Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

With Orc and Human blood running through their veins, Half-Orcs partially resemble the classic Tolkien-esque creatures. They're physically mighty, and they may have visible teeth and green-ish skin.

Their famed physical might is realized through their Relentless Endurance and Savage Attacks. The first ability means that, should a Half-Orc be downed in battle, they can immediately bounce back with one HP. Savage Attack, meanwhile, lets them roll an additional attack die whenever they land a critical hit - perfect for massive bursts of damage.

Like the Half-Elf, the Half-Orc was left out of the 2024 rules update. However, you can still shoehorn them into your games thanks to backwards compatibility. Whether you use their associated ability score increase or not, Half-Orcs are best suited to melee-based martial classes.

Here's a complete guide to the DnD Half-Orc that can tell you more.

Human

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 in all stats, or +1 in two stats plus a feat and skill (2014 rules only)
Best forAll
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

DnD Human characters are variable and adaptable folks, who ambitiously explore the land for both personal gain and altruistic devotion. Their lives are short, but their empires are enormous.

Humans are by far the most versatile of the common species. The 2014 version gives you complete control over your ability score increases, and the popular Variant Human gains a feat for free straight out of the gate.

In the 2024 rules, every character gains a free DnD 2024 feat at level one, but the Human can choose a second feat. They also start with an extra skill proficiency, and they gain Inspiration whenever they finish a long rest. Whichever version of the Human you're planning to use, they're an excellent choice for basically any class.

Learn more in our DnD Human species guide.

Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two stats or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Cleric, Fighter
SourcebookPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

While they're stereotyped as villains in a lot of fantasy media (including past editions of D&D), the Orc 5e has as much right to be a heroic adventurer as anyone else. The Half-Orc's large teeth, green skin, and physical might are all inherited from this species.

An Orc is best known for their imposing strength. Like the Half-Orc, this is represented by the Relentless Endurance ability, which lets them drop to one hit point instead of zero if they are downed in combat. Additionally, Adrenaline Rush lets them dash as a bonus action, Rogue-style, and it gives the Orc temporary HP equal to their proficiency bonus.

Orcs are a natural choice for Strength-based martial builds, though always going for Strength-based builds might start to feel a bit same-y after a while. If you want to shake it up, any fragile spellcaster would appreciate abilities that help them to avoid death.

Tiefling

SizeMedium or Small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWarlock, Sorcerer, Wizard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tieflings have a unique appearance, thanks to their horns, tails, and vibrantly colored skin. These traits come from their ancestry, as somewhere along the line a devil, demon, or yugoloth joined or afflicted their family. This heritage also provides them with resistance to certain DnD damage types and extra spellcasting abilities.

While there are a vast number of Tiefling variants in D&D's many books, the 2024 variant of 5e presents three. Abyssal Tieflings are resistant to poison damage, and they learn Poison Spray, Ray of Sickness, and Hold Person. Chthonic Tieflings are resistant to necrotic damage, and they learn Chill Touch, False Life, and Ray of Enfeeblement. Finally, Infernal Tieflings have fire resistance, and they'll learn Fire Bolt, Hellish Rebuke, and Darkness.

Learn more in our Tiefling 5e and DnD 2024 Tiefling guides.

Aarakocra

SizeMedium
Speed25ft (walking); 50ft (flying while not wearing medium or heavy armor)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Elemental Evil Player's Companion (2015)

The standout feature of the bird-like Aarakocra is their flight. With a large pair of feathered wings sprouting from their back, they were the first playable D&D race that could fly, letting them soar above enemies to pick them off from afar. They have a natural +2 Dexterity and +1 Wisdom increase, and they also sport a pair of talons that let you deal damage equal to 1d4 + your Strength modifier.

Given their natural Dex increase, an Aaarakocra can make a brilliant DnD Ranger, especially if paired with the Archery fighting style to make use of their mobility. The DnD Rogue is also a good choice, as Flight lets you hop about hiding places with even more ease. If you want a more martial build, go for a DnD Fighter specializing in Finesse weapons. Flight will help you traverse the battlefield.

For a full run-through of the best Aarakocra names, classes, and builds, check out our full Aarakocra 5e species guide.

Astral Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forBard
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The Astral Elf 5e comes from literal, actual space (or the Astral Plane, as D&D calls it). They have many of the standard Elf's abilities, including Darkvision, advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and the ability to go into a trance rather than sleep. Starlight Step also lets them teleport 30 feet as a bonus action, and they're naturally proficient in Perception.

The Astral Trance is a bit different from the respite that other Elves get. Whenever you finish a trance, you gain proficiency with one skill and weapon/tool from the Player's Handbook. You can switch these every time you take a DnD long rest - perfect for the party Skill Monkey. 

Autognome

SizeSmall
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAll
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The fifth edition Spelljammer books gave us the Autognome 5e, and these pint-sized automatons are suitable for pretty much any class.

Their metal bodies give them a base armor class of 13 + your Dexterity modifier, even without armor. That's handy for anyone who isn't relying on Strength or heavy armor to protect them. Plus, the excellent 'Built for Success' ability lets you add 1d4 to any attack roll, ability check, or saving throw you make, and you can do so multiple times per day.

The Autognome's remaining abilities are a bit situational - the ability to spend Hit Dice when someone casts mending on you, plus two extra tool proficiencies and the ability to remain conscious while resting. However, this species remains an unusual yet competent all-rounder.

Bugbear

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forBarbarian, Monk, Warlock
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Once one of the most recognizable DnD monsters, members of the Bugbear 5e race are also available as player-character options. They're the hairy, stocky cousins of goblins, and they have a little bit of Feywild magic to help them with skills like stealth.

As well as being proficient in stealth, Bugbears can deal a Surprise Attack (and an extra 2d6 damage) to any creature that hasn't taken a turn yet in combat. While a Rogue might seem like an obvious choice for a Bugbear, that Surprise Attack is useful for pretty much any class in battle. Bugbears also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, but that's less relevant to choosing the right class for your build.

For full details on how you can become a big ol' Bugbear, check out our complete Bugbear 5e species guide.

Centuar

Size40ft
SpeedMedium
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Guildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

These half-humanoid, half-horse Fey creatures have an affinity with nature - and a powerful hind kick. As a Centaur 5e, you'll often be charging into battle - meaning that you'll move 30ft into melee range, hit with your weapons, and then get a Hooves attack with your bonus action. Your hooves are pretty hefty, dealing 1d6 plus your Strength modifier as an unarmed attack.

Centaurs can also choose to have proficiency in Animal Handling, Nature, Medicine, or Survival thanks to their Fey ties. They've got a superior carrying capacity to other creatures of their size, but please don't ask them to climb anything. The hooves make it very difficult. The hooves also limit your optimal class choices - you're best off playing frontline martial classes.

Changeling

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRogue, Bard
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019); Eberron: Forge of the Artificer (2026)

A Changeling 5e has the power to completely alter their appearance as an action. Their ancestry essentially means that they have constant access to the Disguise Self spell, only with guaranteed success. As you can imagine, this means that Changelings excel in social situations - and sneaky subterfuge.

When you create a Changeling character, you can choose two extra skill proficiencies from Deception, Insight, Intimidation, or Persuasion. These additional Charisma-based skills, combined with that powerful shapeshifting ability, make the Changeling ideal for two character types in particular: the sneaky Rogue and the performative Bard.

Deep Gnome

SizeSmall
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Elemental Evil Player's Companion (2015)

Technically, the Deep Gnome 5e is a subrace of the regular Gnome species. However, depending on which books you're reading, you can also find complete rules for a separate Deep Gnome species. Whichever mechanics you plan to use, the basic concept is the same - these are Gnomes born in and shaped by the Underdark.

These Gnomes are tricksy, so their natural ability to cast Disguise Self and Nondetection come in handy. Similarly, they'll get great use out of the Svirfneblin Camouflage feature, which gives them advantage on Stealth checks a certain number of times per long rest. Lastly, your Deep Gnome will be naturally resistant to magic, so they have advantage on Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws against spells.

The Deep Gnome's features complement almost any class in D&D. We'd recommend playing whichever strikes your fancy - though, if you're looking to optimize at every possible turn, the Ranger and the Rogue get the most from the Svirfneblin mix of stealth and sorcery.

Dhampir

SizeMedium or small
Speed35ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Ranger, Monk
SourcebooksRavenloft: The Horrors Within (2026)

A Dhampir is a humanoid of another species that's reached a state of undeath most commonly associated with vampires. Perhaps one of those monsters transformed your Dhampir, or maybe they inherited the curse in some other dark way. Either way, they're almost unrecognizable in their new, undead form.

Your new features include 60 feet of Darkvision, a climbing speed equal to your walking speed (which you can use hands free from level 3 onwards!), and a tasty Vampiric Bite that lets you deal damage and regain HP with your fangs. Plus, the Trace of Undeath means you have Resistance to Necrotic damage.

The original version of the Dhampir from 2021's 'Van Richten's Guide to Ravenloft' was a 'lineage', a modified version of another race. It kept their skill proficiencies and unusual speed types (flying, climbing, etc.), but all other rules were replaced with that of a Dhampir. And unlike the 2026 Dhampir, it didn't need to breathe!

Learn more in our Dhampir 5e guide.

Dracthyr

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forFighter, Barbarian, Druid, Sorcerer
SourcebooksWorld of Warcraft (2026)

Dracthyr are a species specific to World of Warcraft, but their draconic appearance and powers could appeal to any D&D player. In fact, these big lizards have one thing your common garden Dragonborn doesn't: permanent wings. Along with 60 feet of Darkvision, you have wings that allow you to reduce fall damage and glide as you drop.

These wings, along with your tail, can be used to Shove creatures as a bonus action. Plus, from level five, you gain a Fly Speed equal to your speed for 10 minutes. Beyond the power of flight, Dracthyr also have a humanoid form they can shape-shift into to avoid detection.

None of these powers will revolutionize your character build - not even flight, which is already pretty easily accessible by level five. Still, some classes don't have much use for their bonus actions and would appreciate the added agility - Fighters, Barbarians, Druids, Sorcerers, and so on.

Draenei

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forCleric, Warlock, Bard, Ranger, Sorcerer
SourcebooksWorld of Warcraft (2026)

Draenei are a World of Warcraft species, a peaceful humanoid community best recognized by their blue-purple skin and goat-like features (horns, tail, hooves). In D&D, Draenei come with your standard 60 feet of Darkvision, plus the power to regain Heroic Inspiration when they cast a spell (though only once per rest). Draenei characters also have one of four specific lineages that decides damage resistances and what innate spells you gain as you level up.

Regular Draenei are resistant to necrotic damage and have access to Spare the Dying, Healing Word, and Prayer of Healing. Krokul are resistant to Poison damage, adding Poison Spray, Ray of Sickness, and Hold Person to their catalog. Lightforge resist Radiant Damage and know Sacred Flame, Guiding Bolt, and Aid. Last comes Man'ari: resistant to Fire damage and capable of casting Fire Bolt, Hellish Rebuke, and Darkness.

Duergar

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Paladin
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide (2015)

Digital versions and later printings of the Spelljammer books changed this to let you glide horizontally up to your walking speed if you're falling at least ten feet above the ground.

In both versions, Hadozees can also use their Dexterous Feet to manipulate objects, pick up Tiny objects, or interact with doors. SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018)

The Shadar-kai 5e is a species of Elf native to the Shadowfell. Their appearance and abilities have been altered by life in this grim and dark plane, and many of them pledge service to its most powerful deity, The Raven Queen.

In fact, all Shadar-kai have the Blessing of the Raven Queen, an ability that allows them to teleport as a bonus action. After level three, this even grants the Shadar-kai resistance to all damage types for a turn.

As creatures of the night, they're also naturally resistant to necrotic damage and able to see in the dark. And because they're Elves they share many species benefits with their cousins - trance resting, keen senses, fey ancestry, and so on.

Fully customizable ability score increases, plus several free teleports per long rest, mean that the Shadar-kai is an excellent option for any class. If you want to fully optimize, aim for a class that can't already cast Misty Step but would benefit from hopping in and out of melee range.

Shifter

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores-
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

The Shifter 5e race is often called the 'weretouched' thanks to their lycanthrope ancestors. Since they're only part were-beast, they still have a humanoid appearance, but perhaps with a slightly more bestial look. However, they can also partially transform into a werewolf-like form, giving them some formidable battle abilities.

Their Shifting ability gives this species one of several beastly forms, which come with one of four different abilities. Big beastly shifters get Beasthide, granting temporary hit points and a +1 to the Shifter's armor class.

The other options are Longtooth, giving an unarmed fang attack, Swiftstride, granting extra speed and letting you move without triggering opportunity attacks when an enemy stops five feet from you, and Wildhunt, which gives an advantage on Wisdom checks and prevents close-up attacks against you being made with advantage.

Plenty of these powers would benefit a canny martial character, but I can also picture a caster using Swiftstride to get out of trouble.

Simic Hybrid

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Constitution, +1 any other stat
Best forBarbarian, Monk
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

A Simic Hybrid 5e is a humanoid who has been infused with the traits of animals (usually amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, or fish) transforming them into a unique species. Apart from Darkvision, Simic Hybrids only gain one species feature, but they manage to do a lot with it.

All Simic Hybrids start play with either: a climbing speed; a swimming speed and the ability to breathe underwater; or the power to sprout fins that can glide and reduce fall damage. Later, at level five, these characters can choose a different option from this list - or they can pick from a pile of new powers.

This includes basic bonuses like a +1 to your armor class, as well as some more elaborate options. Some Simic Hybrids can spray acid as an action, with the 2d10 damage dealt increasing as they gain level ups.

Others can grow two entirely new appendages, which are perfect for making unarmed strikes and grapples as a bonus action. This used to make the species perfect for Monks, but the 2024 version of the class can perform these feats anyway - so we'd stick to builds that have less to do with their bonus actions.

Tabaxi

SizeMedium
Speed30ft walking and climbing
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forRogue, Monk
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

All Tabaxi were created by the feline Cat Lord, but two of them are rarely alike. Despite the huge variation in appearances and abilities, there are two things that all Tabaxi excel in - agility and stealth.

For example, all Tabaxi have the power to move double their usual speed on a turn (though they'll need to spend a turn standing still to restore that power). Their cat-like claws offer an alternative unarmed attack method, dealing 1d6 plus their Strength modifier in damage.

Plus, these cunning cats all have proficiency in Perception and Stealth. Combine this with 30 feet of climbing speed, and you've got an excellent species for Scout characters.

Check out our Tabaxi 5e species guide for more details. 

Thri-kreen

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue, Fighter
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The Thri-kreen 5e is a giant space bug with four arms and telepathic powers. That's a concept that's bound to inspire plenty of interesting D&D characters. Plus, thanks to the Thri-kreen's funky arms, they have a lot of potential for interesting character builds.

Your Secondary Arms ability lets you use your two smaller arms to manipulate objects, interact with doors and containers, pick up tiny objects, or wield light weapons. That last one is key - you can now wield weapons and shields with hands left over for spellcasting, extra weapons, and so on.

Tortle

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forDruid, Ranger
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Explorer's Guide to Wildemount (2020); The Tortle Package (2017)

The Tortle 5e race may look like a tortoise, but there's nothing slow or dull about them. They're a particularly hardy species, with a natural armor class of 17 (though they can't wear regular armor). A Tortle gains even more defensive power from their signature shell, which they can retreat into to gain advantage on Strength and Constitution rolls.

Tortles can choose from plenty of Wisdom-based and Scout-friendly skill proficiencies. Combine this with their extra defenses, and you've got a species that can make your standard Druid or Ranger build far more durable.

To learn more, check out our DnD Tortle 5e guide.

Triton

SizeMedium
Speed30ft walking, 30ft swimming
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2018)

If you're playing a sea-faring campaign, the Triton 5e is a handy ally to have. Their Amphibious nature means they can breathe air and water, and Emissary of the Sea lets them share basic ideas with creatures that have a swimming speed.

Most of the Triton's unique features offer basic utility. Darkvision is always nice to have, and Guardian of the Depths grants resistance to cold damage. Plus, thanks to Control Air and Water, you can cast Fog Cloud, Gust of Wind, and Water Walk (spell slots optional).

These spells aren't going to break any character builds, and they don't push the Triton towards any particular class. If you're planning to play a Triton, you're probably not planning to power-build anyway - so pick the class that calls to your water-loving heart.

Vedalken

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Intelligence, +1 Wisdom
Best forWizard, Artificer
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

Vedalken 5e are partially amphibious creatures who, apart from their blue skin and lack of hair, closely resemble tall humans. Their most powerful ability isn't particularly flavorful, but it has an explosive mechanical effect. Vedalken have advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws, meaning they're particularly well-defended against magical effects.

Vedalken can also breathe underwater for up to one hour (once per long rest), but this ability pales in comparison with that first trait. Protection against magic is a buff for pretty much any D&D character, after all.

If you need help narrowing down your choices, look to the Vedalken's proficiencies for suggestions. The species is proficient in an extra tool, plus one skill from this list: Arcana, History, Investigation, Medicine, Performance, and Sleight of Hand. This implies a slight advantage for Intelligence-based casters and skill-focused characters - though a Vedalken Barbarian is still perfectly viable.

Verdan

SizeSmall or medium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Constitution
Best forSorcerer, Warlock, Bard
SourcebooksAcquisitions Incorporated (2019)

Introduced by Acquisitions Incorporated, the Verdan 5e evolved from goblinoids, though they're often confused for Half-Elves. Whatever their origin, they're best known for their ability to speak telepathically with any creature they can see within 30 feet.

Verdan are also proficient in Persuasion, as well as Wisdom and Charisma saving throws. They're an excellent choice for Charisma casters, though many characters could take advantage of that extra protection against spells.

We'd recommend choosing the Verdan if your preferred class is a bit squishy. Their Black Blood Healing ability allows them to reroll a 1 or 2 on a Hit Dice roll, which will help keep you on your feet between fights.

Warforged

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Constitution, +1 one other score
Best forArtificer, Barbarian, Cleric
SourcebooksEberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

Members of the Warforged 5e race were once mindless automaton soldiers in the DnD setting of Eberron, but at some point, they gained sentience. Now they're ready to join an adventuring party, armed with their newfound emotions and an artificial body that's ideal for soaking up damage.

Warforged don't need to do pesky mortal things like eat, drink, breathe, or sleep, but they do require rest and healing like any other humanoid. Being made of wood and metal, they're less affected by poisons and they're blessed with a boosted armor class. They can also meld their DnD armor of choice to their body so enemies can't remove it.

To learn more about the Warforged 5e, here's our full guide to the species. 

Yuan-ti

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Part human and part snake, the Yuan-ti 5e can often be distinguished by their serpent eyes, noses, or tongues. These snake-like features come with plenty of perks, including Darkvision, resistance to poison damage, and advantage on rolls against the poisoned condition.

Yuan-ti also gain serpentine spellcasting powers, meaning they can cast Poison Spray, Suggestion, and Animal Friendship (though that last one only works on snakes).

Any adventurer can benefit from the Yuan-ti's handy resistances, but these species traits are a little underwhelming, and none lend themselves well to a particular class. If we were going purely on flavor, we'd make a Swarmkeeper Ranger who can summon an army of slithering friends.

Got a D&D character in mind already? Here are the best DnD campaigns and DnD one shots you could play them in. We can also recommend some other tabletop RPGs to try if you want to go beyond D&D.

title: Pokémon TCG Flowing Fists release date revealed - but which Mega Evolutions still need cards?
content:
On Thursday, the Pokémon company announced that the release date for the next Pokémon set, Flowing Fists, is February 6 2027. It also showed off four new Mega Evolution ex cards from the set, joining 45 Mega Evolutions that have received cards since October 2025; but there are still 44 Mega Evolutions (47 if you count some niche variant forms) unaccounted for!

The Pokemon Company's announcement revealed that Mega Evolution versions of Absol Z, Glimmora, Lucario Z and Garchomp Z will be available in Flowing Fists. On the same day, Pokémon Beach revealed the complete main set card list for the Japanese version of the set, Aura Seeker, which confirmed they're the only Mega Evolutions in the set.

The four revealed cards are very interesting. Mega Lucario Z has a very cheap attack that does excellent damage against Pokémon ex; Mega Absol Z is a hate piece that can stop your opponent using special energy or Stadium cards as soon as it's able to attack; Mega Garchomp Z has two simple ways to do lots of damage (and a theoretically absurd maximum damage, if you have a way to load up your discard pile); and Mega Gimmora ex chooses two of your opponent's Pokémon and puts them one good attack away from dying.

1/4

Once Flowing Fists is out, there'll be cards for 49 Mega Evolution ex Pokémon. We don't know exactly how many more Pokémon sets there will be in the Mega Evolution era, but if the Pokémon company wants to release every Mega Evolution, it's going to take a while! title: From the archives: Star Wars X-Wing's scope, not ease, makes it the best gateway wargame
content:
From the archives: This article was originally posted on March 25, 2021.

Reams of rules, esoteric lore, unwavering commitment to historical accuracy, loads of dice, and miniatures more detailed than the images displayed on an 8K TV: wargames can be truly beastly. But they're not off-limits. Many small skirmish games have sprung up in the wake of the more gargantuan Warhammer 40k or Flames of War, acting as a bridge between the casual board game crowd and the miniatures wargaming space. Ask any keen tabletop-goer the best of these go-to entry-points, and one title will likely crop up again and again - Star Wars: X-Wing.

It's become a cliché. Carrying a globally-recognized license, played using pre-painted miniatures, and boasting a rules system that gives all other dogfighting games a run for their money, X-Wing might just be the safest wargame ever created. It's mechanically straightforward, and its systems intuitive. Even if you've never seen a d8 before, you won't have too much trouble whizzing starships about and firing blasters in frenetic firefights. Put tersely: it's a simple game.

But that does the game a disservice. X-Wing isn't the best beginner wargame because it's simple, but because it has the potential to be complex. Far from offering a diluted miniatures skirmish that dumbs down detail and passes over opportunities for intricacy, X-Wing has all the opportunity for astute stratagems and micro-managed squad customization that you'd expect from a miniatures game. But it hands these to you gradually and organically, rather than dumping an impenetrable system of demanding nuance onto your shoulders from the off.

And I don't just mean its price tag. Sure, you can build a full-point squadron without emptying your wallet of too many shiny pennies, but it's in X-Wing's core gameplay that its ability to entice new players, while fostering their deeper engagement with its core wargaming tenets, really shines.

Take the game's upgrade cards - equippable boons that grant new ship abilities and stat alterations. In some sense, this is where the real meat of strategy enters the game.

Combining upgrades to bolster your ships' strengths, and diminish their weaknesses, while concocting a specialist squadron of units that are complementary, and don't adversely renege on each other's specialties, is no easy task. Buffing your Tie Fighter's bullseye arc so it instantly destroys any vessel that has the misfortune of landing directly in front of it, or pimping your B-Wing so you can perform evasive maneuvers like it's second nature, is as fun as it is challenging.

But also fun is grabbing whatever upgrade cards are to hand, and throwing them onto your ship in a flurry of ill-thought glee. Put that R5 Astromech on that Y-Wing, equip that Tie Defender with those Ion Pulse Missiles. Why the hell not? X-Wing lets you customize your ships in unthinking abandon, but never punishes poor planning. There's enough room to rigorously strategize your combat technique and set a plan of action, as well as gradually experiment with the game's possibilities, as you grapple with how, and when, to use the options available to you.

Part of this comes through the game's persistent action. Your ship is permanently open to fire, vulnerable in the expanse of space. Sure, there might be a little debris for you to hide behind, but it's as deadly to the hull of your ship as it is helpful. You might have the tail end of an enemy ship nicely lined up in your sights, but what are the chances they'll whack out that Koiogran turn and blast you in the face, too?

A small play area and constant opportunities for daring maneuvers make for some truly action-focused skirmishes, in which another chance to test out whatever haphazard mixture of upgrades cards you've picked, or contrived tactic is up your sleeve, is never far away. X-Wing encourages brazen experimentation, rather than tactical-formula-following.

When piloting your way around asteroids and narrowly escaping the range of your enemy ships, the game hands you enough unexpected happenings that there's simply not enough room to predetermine your opponents' moves wholesale. It's pointless planning a watertight strategy, but better to test out new ideas with each match. Fundamentally, X-Wing isn't a game of shrewd strategic planning, but one of reactive ploys and experimentation, as you explore the scope of its systems.

And that makes for a superb introduction to wargames. No need to study stacks of upgrades or internalize concrete tactics, the game lets you pick an idea, have a run with it, and iterate upon your strategy. Learn what works through the throes of the dogfight, and adjust your starship tactics accordingly.

And, if you'd allow just one minor (or excessive) reach, this principle of offering players scope for development through direct engagement with the game's systems is best captured symbolically: by paint of its minis.

X-Wing's pre-painted miniatures make that jump into tabletop wargaming all the simpler for players not keen on learning the intricacies of drybrushing, or scared of the hit their wallet might take from a collection of Citadel paints. Many X-Wing vets do paint their miniatures. Once you appreciate the difference a green strip across your Corvette can make, you can whip out that brush, apply a few thin coats, before going crazy, and painting your fleet in some gaudy color scheme. The option is there, and while you don't have to jump in right away, you'll find yourself getting a little more comfortable with the idea of a deliberate makeover the more you play.

And that's the heart of X-Wing's appeal. It's a simple game, easy to pick up, but offers such breadth and scope as to ease any budding wargamer into the hobby. It's the potential for X-Wing to play as a complex game of squad-specialization, multi-turn strategic planning, and calculated maneuvers, while operating as an instant action dogfighter, that makes it perfect for introducing new players to the hobby.

Want to share how you got into wargaming? Join like-minded fans for a chat in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Warhammer 40k lore - the Blood Ravens
content:
The Blood Ravens are a loyalist Space Marine chapter, but their past is shrouded in mystery, and their present is tainted by the sting of corruption. The protagonists of the Dawn of War videogames and novels, their origins are lost, and the chapter has a voracious appetite for lost secrets.

The Blood Ravens were invented specifically for Dawn of War - it's likely that the process of developing them involved a lot of back and forth between the developers in Relic Entertainment and the Warhammer studio in Games Workshop. Fans may have expected one of the more established Space Marine chapters to star in (at the time) the best Warhammer 40k game ever made, but it was a smart choice, giving the developers lots of freedom to tell stories where significant characters could die horribly!

Blood Ravens primarch and founding

The Blood Ravens do not know who their primarch is, nor when they were founded. Their earliest records begin in M37, with all previous archives lost. They are unlikely to be a second founding Chapter, since the breaking of the legions was an event of profound political importance for the post-Heresy Imperium, cultural importance for the Astartes, and later religious importance for the Cult of the Emperor.

This means the Blood Ravens were likely founded by an act of the Lords of Terra much later, using geneseed tithed from one of the loyalist legions. By dint of numbers, and the stability of their geneseed, the Ultramarines are the most likely founding chapter.

The fact they don't suffer from the Black Rage makes it almost impossible that they're Blood Angels' successors (though the fate-cursed Lamenters appear immune), and before the Era Indomitus and the Ultima founding, there were notoriously few Dark Angels and Space Wolves successors.

After the opening of the Great Rift and the start of the Indomitus Crusade, the Blood Ravens were contacted by the Adeptus Custodes Emissaries Imperatus and presented with the secret knowledge needed to create Primaris Space Marines. This gave the chapter's apothecarion and librarium a fresh source of research for information about their genetic origins - but what they have discovered remains unknown outside their secretive conclaves.

The Great Father

While the Blood Ravens' origins are lost, they do have a legend of an important founding figure - the Father Librarian, or Great Father, Azariah Vidya. When the events of this tale are supposed to have occurred is unknown - it may have been M37, or millennia earlier.

Azariah was chief librarian when the chapter was still young. A campaign in the Gothic sector against the forces of Chaos - which no other Imperial records corobrate as having occurred - took a turn for the worse. An initially disorganized Chaos uprising proved to be dangerously organized, and Blood Ravens strike forces were caught in ambush after ambush. The Chapter Master and Master of Sanctity were both slain, leaving Azariah in command.

Vidya's strategy would be foundational to the Blood Raven's way of war afterwards. Far from launching a bellicose (and likely doomed) counterattack, he prioritized gathering intelligence - and, many suggested, employing his psychic powers of clairvoyance - to probe the enemy. He committed the bulk of Imperial forces to performing delaying actions while he developed a plan to counterattack.

The Blood Angels' retribution was sudden and decisive, striking at multiple locations which all, superficially, appeared to be immaterial, yet proved to be vital staging posts for traitor forces. The campaign was short and extremely bloody. Inquisitorial investigations later concluded the Chaos campaign had been masterminded by the Alpha Legion.

Vidya was feted by the Secret Masters of the Chapter and appointed to become Chapter Master, a role he fulfilled for several centuries. His thirst for knowledge was instilled in the chapter, and it has one of the most comprehensive archives of any Space Marine chapter - from M37 onwards, at least.

Blood Ravens organisation

The Blood Ravens are a Codex-compliant chapter, following Roboute Guillman's tactical edicts. The one unusual aspect of their organization is their extremely large Librarius, known as the Ordo Psykana.

The Ordo Psykana is fairly autonomous, acquiescing to the wishes of the Chapter Master sometimes but often determining its own priorities about where to commit its troops. There are so many of them that the chapter is able to field entire squadrons of librarians when required. The Librarius is also either more powerful, or simply more confident in its abilities, than most. A Blood Ravens Lexicanum - the lowest rank of librarian - is permitted to pilot a warship through the warp in place of a navigator, something that most chapters reserve for far more senior librarians, if they permit it at all..

Chapter Master Gabriel Angelos

The Blood Ravens are currently lead by Gabriel Angelos. A native of the civilized world Cyrene in the Korianis Sector, he entered the Planetary Defence Force while still a youth, becoming a leader even before reaching adolescence. He entered the chapter's Blood Trials and was accepted as an initiate, rising rapidly to the rank of Captain.

He returned to Cyrene as a captain, this time searching for recruits - but the Blood Trials were cut short. The planet had become enmeshed in heretical anti-Imperial ideas, including free trade with xenos, unsanctioned psykers, and even democracy. Angelos condemned the planet to exterminatus. He went to the trouble of seeking out his own father, a former Guardsman, in hopes of saving him - only to discover that he supported the rebels. He executed his father himself.

Angelos' career with the Blood Ravens has been eventful, to say the least. He faced Ork invasion, the machinations of the Alpha Legion, and betrayal by his friend Librarian Isador Akios on Tartarus. Events on Rane's Paradise cause the awakening of Necrons, and his quest to stop them saw him travel through the webway and retrieve a legendary Blade of Vaul.

Angelos was pivotal in the intra-chapter civil war that constituted the second and third Aurelian Crusade. What began as a revolt by the planetary governor of Aurelia was soon revealed to be a plot by the Black Legion, aided by chapter master and chief librarian Azariah Kyras.

Gabreil slew the Chaos lord Eliphas the Inheritor at the culmination of the second crusade, and led the loyalist Blood Ravens against the corrupted Chapter Master in the third. Though ultimately victorious against Kyras, Angelos lost both legs and his right eye in the battle. He was elevated to the post of Chapter Master in recognition of his pivotal role saving the soul of the chapter.

Blood Ravens home world and recruitment

While the Blood Ravens' original homeworld is not known, they did once maintain a Fortress Monastery on the ice world Aurelia, capital of the sub-sector of the same name. However the planet was rendered uninhabitable by a warpstorm in the 40th millennium, resulting in the Blood Ravens becoming a fleet based Chapter.

The Blood Ravens flagship is the Omnis Arcanum, a battle barge. As well as a powerful ship of the line, this is the site of the vast archives of the Librarium Sanctorum.

The chapter recruits from a variety of worlds within the Aurelia sub-sector, which have a higher than ordinary density of pyskers, and their initiation rites favor those with psychic potential. Like the Grey Knights they have a direct arrangement with the Adeptus Astra Telepathica that allows them to recruit from the Scholastica Psykana on Terra.

Following the back-to-back degradation of the Acheron campaign, the three Aurelian Crusades, and the Kaurava campaign, the chapter was in dire need of reinforcement and repair. Angelos gave the order to regroup in sub-sector Aurelia and begin Blood Trials to find aspirants on every world where the Blood Ravens had recruitment rites.

This plan was thrown into disarray by the opening of the Great Rift, causing the Astronomicon to dim and flicker out. The Aurelia sub-sector was stranded in Imperium Nihilus, with astropathic communication more perilous than ever and warp navigation restricted to short, almost blind leaps. Had the Custodes not discovered the chapter's seventh company to deliver the gift of the Primaris technology, the chapter may have been rapidly driven to extinction.

Blood Ravens battlecry

The Blood Ravens oldest battle cry is 'knowledge is power - guard it well'. Since Gabriel Angelos' elevation to chapter master, 'none shall find us wanting' has been widely adopted. The second company favors 'victory over death', following their victory against the Necrons on the planet Kronus.

Are the Blood Ravens Thousand Sons successors?

The Blood Ravens probably aren't Thousand Sons successors… probably. This has been a popular fan theory since they were introduced; their psychic might is prodigious, and they're obsessed with secrets and uncovering their lost origins, which is prime T'zeentch behaviour.

The Thousand Sons are perhaps the least likely legion to have surviving loyalists. Magnus the Red effectively bartered away his entire Legion's souls long before the Horus Heresy, unknowingly pledging them to T'zeentch in his efforts to halt the flesh change. It takes an awful lot of plot contrivances to escape from that fate.

But we got such a character in the Horus Heresy novels - Revuel Arvida. Note that name - it's not quite an anagram of Azariah Vidya, but it is reminiscent. A member of the precognitive Corvidae cult, Arvida arrived late to the sacking of Prospero, meaning he never joined the rest of the legion in the Warp.

He encountered the White Scars when they visited the ruins of Prospero, joining them in their battle against the Warmaster. Despite forming a close bond, he refused their offers to be inducted into the legion, seeing an important destiny associated with the raven symbol on his pauldron - he even uttered the Blood Ravens' motto, "Knowledge is power". That's a hell of a Blood Raven-y hint!

But, the flesh change gradually overcame Arvida as he assisted the White Scars in their journey to Terra. He was almost reduced to a mewling chaos spawn. At the primarch Jaghatai's request, Malcador the Sigilite was able to stabilize him by fusing him with a fragment of the soul of Magnus the Red that was left behind in the wreckage of Magnus' infiltration of the throne room. Arvida was reborn as Ianus.

This almost certainly means that Arvida became Janus, the first Supreme Grand Master of the Grey Knights: he fits the bill perfectly. It remains conceivable that the myth and the origin overlap - that Supreme Grand Master Janus had a role to play in the foundation or recovery of the Blood Ravens in the guise of Azariah Vidya. Black Library authors like to muddy the waters.

Are the Blood Ravens kleptomaniacs?

The Blood Ravens are meme-infamous for stealing things - this isn't quite accurate. Dawn of War 2 has 394 equippable wargear items, and the writers gave every one a unique description. A tiny minority of them read as suspect.

Blood Ravens armorers claim they received the Pistol of Baal in a ceremonial exchange with the Blood Angels in M37, but the Blood Angels have no records; a Stalker-Pattern bolter that "came to the Blood Ravens" after a Captain served alongside Ultramarines successors (likely the Iron Snakes) in the Sabbat Worlds crusade; the heavy flamer Righteous Inferno is believed to have come from the Adeptus Custodes.

Then there was the expandalone sequel Chaos Rising, where the item list rose to 844, and the writers cut loose. The Blood Ravens have, somehow, acquired the Golden Armor of the Custodes; a Vindicare assassin's Exitus Rifle, apparently left as a gift; even the very same Thunder Hammer and Storm Shield wielded by Blood Angels Blood sergeant Gideon during his chapter's assault on the space hulk Sin of Damnation - that would be the same Space Hulk that features in the board game!.

We could easily attribute the number of relics in the Blood Angels possession to videogame logic. After all in Chaos Rising you can find Forgebreaker, hammer of the Primarch Ferrus Manus, forged by his brother Fulgrim, stolen and corrupted by Perturabo, and one of the most corrupted daemonic artefacts in the Eye of Terror, in a random loot drop.

But the Blood Ravens do, canonically, live up to their namesake bird. They really do collect shiny artifacts - they just don't steal them from their current owners. In White Dwarf 305 (May 2005), Graham McNeill's article 'Index Astartes - Knowledge is Power - The Blood Ravens Space Marines Chapter' states "it is not uncommon for groups of Librarians to be dispatched with an army of servitors and a number of squads of Space.Marines to uncover a lost artefact whose location has been recently unearthed or revealed through ritual divination".

This has caused conflict with the Inquisition, because many of the items they collect are tainted by Chaos. What's more, while the Blood Ravens say "by recovering and destroying the tools of Chaos they deny the Enemy their use" - but they haven't been able to provide satisfactory "proof of the destruction of any of the hundreds of artifacts they are said to have procured". So the loot table in Dawn of War 2: Chaos Rising really is the sort of thing you'll find in the Blood Ravens' vaults!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.
